steps: One record per Wikipedia obsolete occupation, with description and reason text (Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0) and an image hotlinked from Wikimedia Commons with its credit.
census.series: for jobs whose OCC1950 match is exact, IPUMS's weighted category total (seriesSource 'category'); otherwise the title-search estimate, a minimum (seriesSource 'title').
census.series: estimated people per census year; 'reliable' when based on at least 10 sample records. Jobs with fewer than 10 records across all years get no series (likely false matches).

flows[].transitions: for each census pair A->B, where people in the job's OCC1950 category in A were in B; only when the match is exact, or broader with a specific (non-n.e.c.) category at medium/high confidence, at least 100 linked people, and at least 10 sample records with the job's own title in A. Top 8 destinations plus 'Everything else' (which includes suppressed small cells).
flows[].arrivals: the reverse: A jobs of people in the job's category in B (origins limited to working-age people with an occupation in A), requiring the job's title in B's sample.
defaultFlow: index of the pair where the job's estimated workforce fell the most.
categories: OCC1950 codes referenced by flows, with weighted category totals by year (category_counts) and the Wikipedia job they exactly match, for hover cards.
Non-occupational OCC1950 codes relabelled in plain language (e.g. 999 -> 'No occupation listed').

Census jobs (origin 'census') from data/manual/census_jobs.csv: description from the manual table or the first three sentences of the Wikipedia article intro; reason from the manual table (draft flag from its status); image from the article; series and flows from the job's OCC1950 category; endCentury = century of the first census after the peak where the category's share of workers fell below 10% of its peak share (IPUMS public sample counts, 1850-2024). Where the manual table gives earlier_code/earlier_until, that code is used for census years up to earlier_until (series and flows); 'note' explains such quirks on the page.
